title: Alcohol, Drugs & Fatigue
summary: How alcohol, drugs and tiredness affect your riding, how the body handles alcohol, and how to protect yourself and your friends.

sections.heading: Why impairment matters on a motorcycle

blocks.text: Riding takes constant attention, quick judgment and precise control. More than any other factor, alcohol and drugs damage your ability to think clearly and ride skillfully.

items: Alcohol is a major contributor to motorcycle crashes, particularly fatal ones.
As little as one drink can have a significant effect on how you ride. Even a drink or two in your system is enough to impair riding skills.
Judgment and decision-making are affected long before legal limits are reached.

Drinking and drug use are as big a problem for riders as for car drivers, but riders are more likely to be killed or badly injured in a crash. Injuries occur in 90% of motorcycle crashes that involve substance abuse, compared with 33% of such car crashes.
No one is immune, no matter how well they claim to hold their liquor.
Many over-the-counter, prescription and illegal drugs have side effects that raise your risk when riding.
Alcohol and drugs together are more dangerous than either one alone.
Cannabis tends to distort your sense of time, space and speed. That is critical for riders, who must make split-second decisions.
Even where cannabis is legal, riding while impaired by it is not. Riders impaired by cannabis can be convicted of riding under the influence and face similar harsh penalties.

rows: Smoked cannabis
Effects usually start within a few minutes and last about 2 to 4 hours.
Eaten cannabis
Effects can take more than an hour to start and last more than 6 hours.

sections.heading: How alcohol works in your body

blocks.text: Alcohol does not need to be digested like food. It goes straight into the bloodstream and reaches the brain within minutes, slowing both mental and physical functions.

Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) is the amount of alcohol in relation to the blood in your body. The higher your BAC, the more impaired you are. In general, the body can eliminate alcohol at a rate of almost one drink per hour, though other factors affect how much is retained.

rows: Three main factors in BAC
How much alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, and your body weight.
Other factors
Sex, physical condition and food eaten can push BAC even higher.
One drink equals
A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a mixed drink with one 1.5-ounce shot of liquor. All hold about the same amount of alcohol.

blocks.text: Even at one drink per hour, alcohol can still build up in your body, especially for women. That one drink can already affect your skills and judgment.
The faster you drink, the more alcohol builds up. Ignoring other factors, subtract the hours spent drinking from the number of drinks to find the minimum still in your system.

rows: 2 drinks in 1 hour
At least 1 drink still in your blood at the end of that hour.
4 drinks over 2 hours
At least 2 drinks remain (4 - 2). Wait at least 2 more hours before you consider riding.
7 drinks over 3 hours
At least 4 drinks remain (7 - 3). Wait at least 4 more hours before you consider riding.

blocks.text: Waiting one hour per drink is not a guarantee. Tiring after-effects of drinking can remain even after the alcohol is gone.

How sober you look or act does not matter. A breath, blood or urine test usually decides whether you are riding legally. Legal BAC limits vary, with lower limits for riders under 21, so check your state's rule in the State Cheat Sheet. Remember that impairment starts well below any legal limit.
Most states now impose stiff penalties that judges must impose. A conviction for riding under the influence of alcohol or drugs can bring:

items: Mandatory license suspension for a conviction, an arrest, or refusing a breath test.
Heavy fines, usually along with a suspension.
Higher insurance rates: a DUI/DWI conviction can put you in a high-risk category long after the court case ends.
Community service.
Other costs: lawyer fees, lost work time, education programs and getting around without a license.

blocks.text: Alcohol affects your ability to judge your own riding first. You ride worse and worse while believing you ride better and better, so you take bigger risks. The best plan is to keep drinking and riding completely separate.

items: Don't drink. Once you start, your resistance gets weaker.
Setting a drink limit or pacing yourself is a poor alternative at best, because judgment is one of the first things alcohol affects.
Or don't ride. If you have not controlled your drinking, leave the motorcycle so you are not tempted, and arrange another way home.
If you went over your limit, wait until your body has cleared the alcohol and its tiring after-effects.

sections.heading: Step in to protect a friend

blocks.text: Someone who has had too much to drink cannot make a responsible decision, so it is up to others to step in. It feels awkward and you will rarely be thanked at the time, but the alternatives are often worse.

rows: Arrange a safe ride
Offer another way for them to get home.
Slow the pace
Get them involved in other activities instead of drinking.
Keep them there
Use any excuse to keep them off the bike. Serve food and coffee, explain your concerns, and take their key and secure their bike if you can.
Get friends involved
Use peer pressure from a group of friends to intervene.

blocks.text: Riding a motorcycle is more tiring than driving a car, so on a long trip you will tire sooner. Fatigue hurts your control of the bike. Avoid riding when tired.

items: Protect yourself from the elements. Wind, cold and rain wear you out fast. Dress warmly, and a windshield is worth the cost for long-distance riding.
Limit your distance. Experienced riders seldom ride more than about six hours a day.
Take frequent breaks. Stop and get off the motorcycle at least every two hours.
Don't drink or use drugs. Artificial stimulants often cause extreme fatigue or depression when they wear off, and you cannot concentrate.

keyPoints: Alcohol and drugs hurt your riding more than any other factor; even one drink matters.
Riders who crash impaired are more likely than drivers to be killed or badly injured.
BAC depends mainly on how much you drink, how fast, and your body weight; a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine and a mixed drink with a 1.5-ounce shot hold the same alcohol.
Your body eliminates almost one drink per hour at best, so time is critical, and fatiguing after-effects can last longer.
Alcohol damages your judgment of your own riding first, so separate drinking from riding completely.
Mixing alcohol and drugs is worse than either alone; cannabis distorts time, space and speed.
Step in to stop an impaired friend: arrange a ride, keep them there, take their key, get others involved.
Fight fatigue: dress for the weather, ride no more than about six hours a day, and stop at least every two hours.
